Ihsan, a US resident of Palestinian descent, says he was questioned by the Secret Service during a trip to Washington, DC, as a result of his social media posts about Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and the complicity of the US government.

Ihsan told TRT World that he was exercising his constitutional right to free speech and has not done anything unlawful.

He said agents first visited his home in 2024 to ask about his online activity, and that he has since been placed on the Secondary Security Screening Selection list whenever he travels.

Ihsan added that during a recent international trip, agents detained him for several hours and confiscated his phone after he refused to unlock it.

“I think it’s disgusting. But I also look at it as. Here’s a way to educate American society to show them how our rights are being restricted,” Ihsan said.

Is The New Israeli Law Deepening Divisions And Fueling Protests In Gaza?

Tensions are rising in the Gaza Strip as Palestinians take to the streets in Khan Younis and Deir al-Balah to protest a controversial new law passed by Israel.

The legislation introduces the death penalty—by hanging—as a default sentence for Palestinians convicted in military courts of deadly attacks. Critics argue that the law is discriminatory, claiming it targets Palestinians while not applying equally to Jewish Israelis in similar cases.

Mahmoud Abbas has strongly condemned the move, calling it a violation of international law and a step that could further inflame tensions in the region.

The law has also drawn sharp criticism from multiple countries, including Pakistan, Turkey, Egypt, and Saudi Arabia, as well as concerns from Western allies and the European Union.

Palestinians in Gaza react to Israeli death penalty law for Palestinian prisoners

Palestinians in Gaza expressed grave concern and deep sorrow over the passing of a law allowing for the death penalty for Palestinian prisoners charged with terrorism offences in the Israeli Knesset on Monday.

“It is unfair, overbearing and painful,” said Ahmed Al-Ras, a displaced Palestinian in Khan Younis.

The legislation establishes two separate pathways for the death penalty based on national identity. The law makes the death penalty the default sentence for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank who are tried in military courts.
